questions.question: What does `[f() for f in [lambda: i for i in range(3)]]` evaluate to?
options: A NameError because i is out of scope
questions.explanation: Closures look up i when they run, not when they are defined. All three lambdas share the same i, which is 2 after the loop finishes. Binding it as a default argument (lambda i=i: i) fixes this.

questions.question: Which is exactly equivalent to placing `@timed` above `def add(a, b): ...`?
options: Calling timed(add) every time add is called
timed is applied lazily the first time add is called
add = timed(add), executed once when the def statement runs
questions.explanation: Decorator syntax is sugar for rebinding the name to decorator(func), and it runs once at definition time, usually at import, not on every call.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of `functools.wraps` inside a decorator?
options: It copies metadata such as __name__ and __doc__ from the original function onto the wrapper and sets __wrapped__
It makes the wrapper run faster by caching results
It allows the decorator to accept arguments
It prevents the decorator from running at import time
questions.explanation: Without functools.wraps the decorated function reports the wrapper's name and docstring. wraps copies __name__, __doc__, __module__ and __qualname__ and sets __wrapped__, which help() and inspect rely on.

questions.question: For a decorator used as `@retry(times=3)`, how many levels of nested functions are normally needed?
options: One: retry itself is the wrapper
Two: retry returns the wrapper directly
Three: retry(times) returns a decorator, which takes func and returns the wrapper
None: arguments are passed using functools.partial automatically
questions.explanation: retry(times=3) is called first and must return the actual decorator, which receives func and returns the wrapper. So it is retry, then decorator, then wrapper.
